analysis.one_liner: Lets private-sector workers choose paid time off instead of cash overtime pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, employers must pay hourly workers 1.5 times their wage for overtime hours. This bill would let a worker choose, instead, to take 1.5 hours of paid time off for each overtime hour worked. The choice had to be voluntary and recorded in writing, unused time had to be paid out in cash each year, and employers who pressured workers faced penalties. The bill included a five-year expiration date. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who would rather take time off than extra cash — for example, parents who want a day at home more than a bigger paycheck. Employers also gain, because they could satisfy the overtime requirement with scheduling flexibility instead of immediate cash, and unused time could be granted during slow periods.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers wanting time off over cash

how_it_helps.text: Workers could opt to bank one and one-half hours of paid time off for each overtime hour worked, instead of receiving overtime cash. [S2] [S3]
The agreement had to be voluntary, made before the work was performed, and kept on a written or verifiable record — and could not be a condition of employment. [S3]
Employers who intimidated, threatened, or coerced workers over the choice would owe the worker the value of every hour of accrued compensatory time, plus equal liquidated damages. [S3]
Workers could withdraw the agreement at any time and demand cash for all accrued but unused compensatory time, which the employer would have to pay within 30 days. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would give up the current certainty of paying overtime in cash and would face cash-out obligations for unused time each January and whenever a worker quits or is fired — paid at the higher of the rate when earned or the final regular rate.

drawbacks.text: The employer, not the worker, decides when compensatory time may actually be used: a worker's request must be granted only if it does not 'unduly disrupt the operations of the employer.' Time off a worker cannot use is worth less than cash. [S3]

An employer could pay out, over a worker's objection, any accrued compensatory time above 80 hours on 30 days' notice, and could discontinue its compensatory-time policy entirely on 30 days' notice. [S3]

Critics in the labor movement argued that in practice, employers could pressure low-wage workers into accepting time off in place of guaranteed overtime cash — a concern the bill's written-agreement and anti-coercion provisions were meant to answer but could not fully remove.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a genuine option — more time off for parents and caregivers — with real guardrails: a written voluntary agreement, a one-year tenure requirement, annual cash-out of unused time, a 160-hour cap, and liquidated damages for coercion. But the value of time off depends entirely on the employer granting it when the worker needs it, and the employer retained the power to cash out or drop the program on a month's notice. For a worker who needs cash and cannot get the time off approved, the option could leave them worse off than the existing cash guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, which never acted on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Judy Biggert introduced the bill on May 24, 2001, with 32 original cosponsors. [S3] [S5]
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced. [S5]
On July 25, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where no further action was recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: employers kept the current cash-overtime requirement, and workers kept their existing overtime guarantee — but also gained no new option to trade overtime for time off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and the overtime status quo

for.name: Rep. Judy Biggert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Working Families Flexibility Act of 2001 and gave introductory remarks on the House floor. [S3] [S5]

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; never reported the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action beyond sending it to a subcommittee, so it never reached the House floor. [S5]

against.name: AFL-CIO and allied labor unions
against.role: Labor federation opposing private-sector compensatory time
against.what_they_did: Opposed private-sector compensatory-time legislation, arguing employers could pressure workers into accepting time off instead of guaranteed overtime pay.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was almost entirely Republican: 44 of 223 House Republicans signed on alongside 1 of 208 House Democrats, and it advanced nowhere in a House whose committee process it never cleared. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would have let employers satisfy overtime law with paid time off instead of immediate cash, easing scheduling and cash-flow pressures. Whether that ran with or against workers depended on whether the employer actually granted the time off, which the bill left largely to the employer's operations. [S3]

For unionized workplaces, compensatory time could only be provided under the terms of the collective bargaining agreement, keeping unions in control of the arrangement. Unions nonetheless opposed the bill's expansion of comp time to the nonunion workforce. [S3]
